Project Gutenberg is a name that appears only in the licensing and legal boilerplate of this eBook, not as a character. It is an organisation tied to the book's publication: the owner of its trademark, which has agreed to donate royalties to the Project Gutenberg Literary Archive Foundation. It requires royalty payments and refunds under its licence terms.
The listed author of this book, named only in the publication details.

Bram Stoker is the named author of the book, credited on the title page as its writer and as the copyright holder. The only passage shows him as author, and nothing else about his role or nature is given.
A person to whom the book is dedicated as a dear friend; no further role is shown in this passage.
Married Jonathan Harker in Buda-Pesth and keeps his note-book sealed, promising never to open it.
Has typed out her own journal and Jonathan's diary, and is a skilled shorthand writer who admires interviewing.
Teased Van Helsing with her shorthand diary before handing him a typewritten copy, and is admired by him as clever.
Is anxious and intelligent, and has been writing and typing the diaries and papers that document the case.
Acts as secretary at the council and is asked by Van Helsing to keep out of the coming danger.
Keeps her own journal so that Jonathan may read every thought she has, and is kept in the dark about the campaign.
The Sacred Wafer seared a red scar onto her forehead, which she believes marks her as unclean until the Judgment Day.
Under the Count's influence, she now insists on joining the journey, fearing she will be compelled to betray the plans.
Has been hypnotised by Van Helsing each sunset, answering 'darkness, lapping water and creaking wood' to show the boat's position.
Her forehead bears the red scar from the Sacred Wafer, which the vampire women see as a sign she is one of them.

Mina Murray is a young woman who keeps a journal, and her diary entries appear across the early chapters. She is a close friend of Lucy Westenra, and her letters and writings reveal a careful, observant and literate nature. Her later marriage to Jonathan Harker is shown only as an intention, not yet as a settled fact.

Mina Murray is a young woman who keeps a journal and writes letters, and she is a close friend of Lucy Westenra. Her writing shows her to be careful, observant and literate. Jonathan Harker imagines sharing his travel notes with her, but these passages do not describe her as directly involved in his journey.

Mina Murray is a young woman whose letters and journal are written in shorthand and cipher-like form, and who is the person Jonathan Harker most wants to share his travel notes with. Harker writes to her in shorthand so the Count cannot read it, and he keeps her in mind as someone he must protect from the horrors he has seen.

Mina Murray is a young woman and an assistant schoolmistress, engaged to Jonathan Harker, who writes to her in shorthand and keeps a stenographic journal of her own. She is Lucy Westenra's close friend and correspondent, sharing confidences with her. Harker wants to protect her from the horrors he has seen, and he expects to share his travel notes with her.

Mina Murray, married to Jonathan Harker in Buda-Pesth, keeps his note-book sealed, promising never to open it. She is a young assistant schoolmistress and Lucy Westenra's close friend and confidante, sharing secrets and writing to her in shorthand. She practises shorthand and typewriting to help Harker with his work and keeps a private journal of her own, described as a warm, open correspondent.

Mina is a clever, anxious young woman who types, shorthands and keeps journals, documenting the events of the case. She is engaged to, and later married to, Jonathan Harker, and is the close confidante of Lucy Westenra, to whom she writes candidly. Van Helsing admires her cleverness, and she teases him with her shorthand diary before giving him a typewritten copy.

Mina is a clever, anxious young woman who keeps journals and writes letters, and is skilled at shorthand and typing. She is engaged to Jonathan Harker and is the close confidante of Lucy Westenra, to whom she writes openly. Van Helsing has written to her, asking for her help, and she has expressed a willingness to travel to meet him.

Mina Harker, married to Jonathan Harker, is a clever, anxious young woman who types and keeps journals, letters and shorthand records of the case. She is admired by Van Helsing for her intellect, and her companions keep her out of the most dangerous work. She is said to bear a scar on her forehead, which she believes marks her as unclean.

Mina Harker, married to Jonathan Harker, is a clever, anxious young woman who types and keeps journals and shorthand records of the case. Van Helsing admires her intellect, and her companions keep her out of the most dangerous work. She bears a red scar on her forehead, which she believes marks her as unclean.
Shows deep, anguished emotion when he realises Mrs. Westenra unknowingly removed the protective flowers from Lucy's room.
Acts with stern urgency and frenzied determination when fighting death for Lucy, and has been keeping secrets from the others.
Keeps Lucy's papers and letters, and reveals that he is trained as a lawyer as well as a doctor.
Shows a fierce, changeable grief, laughing and weeping together, and says he knows a reason for his sorrow he cannot share.
Says he has read Mina's letters and diary and is grateful to her, and claims to have studied the brain all his life.
Believes Lucy is Un-Dead and resolves to stake her and remove her head, and to take Arthur through the painful truth.
Leaves Seward to travel on to Amsterdam while Mina goes to Seward's house.
Leads the council, describes the vampire's powers and limits, and identifies the Count as a former voivode of the Draculas.
Gently apologises to Mina for reminding her of her ordeal, showing care for her.
Leads the pursuit, questioning shipping men and resolving to meet the Count at Varna.
Gives a theory that the Count is a criminal of child-like mind who repeats the same crimes, and reads Mina's words as a key to his method.
Has destroyed the three female vampires and Dracula's tomb, banishing the Count from it with the Sacred Wafer.

Abraham Van Helsing is an Amsterdam physician, once Dr. Seward's teacher and a close friend, and an expert in obscure diseases. He is a philosopher, metaphysician and scientist with an iron nerve, an open mind, indomitable resolve and a kind heart, and his manner is abrupt and dogmatic. He is called in to examine Lucy Westenra and suspects a hidden cause behind her decline.

Abraham Van Helsing is an Amsterdam physician, once Dr. Seward's teacher and friend, and an expert in obscure diseases. He is a philosopher, metaphysician and scientist with an iron nerve, an open mind and an indomitable resolve, whose manner is abrupt, stern and dogmatic. He is called in to examine Lucy Westenra, suspects a hidden cause behind her decline, and arranges a blood transfusion from Arthur Holmwood.

Van Helsing is an Amsterdam physician and doctor of philosophy, letters and medicine, once a teacher and friend of Dr. Seward. He is stern, abrupt and intense, with an iron will, and he performs Lucy Westenra's blood transfusions while watching over her with frantic urgency. He is withholding his conclusions from the others and speaks a formal, broken English. Lucy's death is said to be only the beginning, and he tells Seward that they must wait and see.

Still alive at this point, though the companion's notes tell of a telegram from Van Helsing announcing the deaths of Mrs. Westenra and Lucy, both buried that day. Abraham Van Helsing is an Amsterdam physician, trained as a lawyer and holding doctorates in philosophy and letters, once a teacher of Dr. Seward. He is stern, intense and urgent, with an iron will, and he runs Lucy's blood transfusions and watches over her himself. He withholds his conclusions, and his grief swings sharply between weeping and laughter.

Abraham Van Helsing is an Amsterdam physician, trained as a lawyer and holding doctorates in philosophy and letters, and once a teacher of Dr. Seward. He is stern, intense and urgent, with an iron will, and his grief swings between sobbing and bursts of laughter. He conducts blood transfusions for Lucy and keeps watch over her himself, and he holds that she is Un-Dead, a belief he has pressed on Seward and on Arthur Holmwood, whom he has told of it and asked to attend.

Abraham Van Helsing is an Amsterdam physician, trained as a lawyer and holding doctorates in philosophy and letters. He is stern, intense and urgent, with an iron will, and his grief swings between sobbing and bursts of laughter. He conducts blood transfusions for Lucy, keeps close watch over her, and holds that she is Un-Dead, a belief he has pressed on Seward and on Arthur Holmwood. He takes a leading part in the drive to stake her, and he reads the prayers for the dead while Arthur drives the stake.

Abraham Van Helsing is an Amsterdam physician, trained as a lawyer, and an older mentor to Dr. Seward, whom he calls his friend John. He is stern, intense and urgent, with an iron will and bushy brows, and his grief swings between sobbing and laughter. He arranges blood transfusions for Lucy, keeps close watch over her, and holds that she is Un-Dead, a belief he presses on Seward and Arthur Holmwood. He is given to strong feeling, sometimes breaking down, and he has a sharp ear for sounds and a knack of sensing what others miss.

Abraham Van Helsing is a physician from Amsterdam, trained also as a lawyer, who takes the lead in the fight over Lucy's illness and presses others to accept his belief that she is Un-Dead. He is stern, urgent and changeable in feeling, with bushy brows and a sharp eye that misses little. He keeps close watch over the sick, arranges blood transfusions, and is respected for his learning and his commanding manner.

A physician from Amsterdam, also trained as a lawyer, who leads the fight over Lucy's illness and presses others to accept his belief that she is Un-Dead. He is stern, urgent and changeable in feeling, with a sharp eye and a commanding manner, and he keeps close watch over the sick. He arranges blood transfusions and is respected for his learning. He insists on secrecy and takes charge of the group's decisions, including the staking of Lucy's body.

A physician from Amsterdam, also trained as a lawyer, who leads the group's fight over Lucy and her Un-Dead state. Stern, urgent and changeable in feeling, with a sharp eye, a noble bearing and a commanding manner, he is respected for his learning, insists on secrecy and takes charge of the group's decisions. He destroys the three female vampires and Dracula's tomb, banishing the Count from it with the Sacred Wafer.
An old frontier town with a stormy past of fires and sieges, where Harker stays at the Golden Krone Hotel.

Bistritz is a town in Transylvania, a post town near the frontier and the Borgo Pass, described as an old, interesting place with a stormy history of fires and a siege. It is the place where the travelling narrator arrives and stays at the Golden Krone Hotel, and it is the post town that Count Dracula named to him.

Bistritz is a post town in Transylvania, near the frontier and the Borgo Pass, described as an old place with a stormy past of fires and a siege. It is where the travelling narrator arrives, stays at the Golden Krone Hotel, and is met by a woman who warns him, and it is the post town that Count Dracula named to him as his travel point.
The hotel in Klausenburgh where Harker spends a night and eats paprika chicken.
A town on Harker's route east, where he stops at the Hotel Royale for the night.
A neighbouring region reached through the Borgo Pass, to which the diligence coach is bound.

Bukovina is a region bordering Transylvania, reached from Bistritz through the Borgo Pass. It is a destination named by Count Dracula and by the coach driver, and the strange driver of the calèche says the Count will bring Harker there, though the passages never show Bukovina as a place Harker actually reaches.
Dracula's castle, which Harker has not yet been able to find on any map and which is named as the destination.

Castle Dracula is a castle in the Carpathian mountains of eastern Transylvania, in a remote and little-known district near the borders of three states. It has no map location a reader can yet pin down, and it is the home of the nobleman Count Dracula, who arranges a visitor's journey to it. The visitor expects to see more of him there.

Castle Dracula is a castle in the wild, little-known Carpathian mountains of eastern Transylvania, near the borders of three states. It is the home of Count Dracula, who arranges a visitor's journey to it and hopes to see more of that visitor there. Its exact location is not found on any map a reader has consulted.

A Transylvanian nobleman who corresponds with Harker in written letters and arranges his journey. His house and servants are feared by the locals, and his carriage driver is a strangely strong and unnatural figure.
An old, tall, clean-shaven man in black with a long white moustache, who welcomes Harker with a cold, unnaturally strong handshake and never eats or drinks in his presence.
Has a strong aquiline face, pale complexion, sharp white teeth, and coarse broad hands with hair on the palms and long pointed nails.
Takes great pride in his noble Szekely and Dracula ancestry and speaks of his house as if he had lived its battles.
Has a powerful hold over Harker, who feels he must rely on the Count for safety while fearing him deeply.
Is the master of three vampiric women who serve his will and whom he forbids from touching Harker.
Can climb down the sheer castle wall face-first like a lizard, moving headfirst along the stones.
Keeps a hidden room in the castle, filled with old gold and chains, and a vault where he sleeps in an earth-filled box.
Lies in his box gorged with fresh blood and appears younger, his hair dark iron-grey, showing a monstrous nature.
Described by Van Helsing as the vampire of the Draculas, a voivode whose cunning and power are feared across many lands.
Is strong enough to handle heavy earth-boxes himself, lifting them as easily as pounds of tea.
Has a scar on his forehead and a waxen, aquiline face; shows terrible, blood-dripping fury when confronted by the company.
Escaped London by ship and had his box shipped; described as tall, thin, pale, with burning eyes and white teeth.
Mina reads him as a criminal type who, when beaten, flees home and returns with better preparation.

Count Dracula is a nobleman of Transylvania whose castle lies in the wild Carpathian mountains, and who arranges Jonathan Harker's journey by letter. He writes courteously, signing himself as Harker's friend, and sends instructions for the coach, hotel and a carriage at the Borgo Pass. Locals at the Golden Krone are said to fear him and refuse to speak of him or his castle.

Count Dracula is a Transylvanian nobleman living in a remote castle in the Carpathians, who corresponds with Jonathan Harker and receives him as a guest. He is tall, courtly and formal, with a cold and unusually strong handshake, and he avoids eating in front of Harker. Locals at the Golden Krone are said to fear him, and the landlord and his wife refuse to speak of him or his castle. He keeps late hours, talking until dawn, and his books and atlas show England with marked locations near London, Exeter and Whitby.

Holding Jonathan Harker prisoner in his castle, having shut him in himself, Count Dracula is a Transylvanian nobleman who lives there alone, with no other servants. He is old and tall, with a long white moustache, sharp canine teeth, and an unnaturally strong grip. He speaks with pride of his house's history, as if he had lived its battles, and he controls wolves with a raised hand. He also reads Harker's letters before they are sent, and he takes Harker's papers and his luggage.

Alive and at large, having been found lying in one of fifty earth-filled boxes in the vault, apparently dead yet warm. Count Dracula is a Transylvanian nobleman, old and tall with a long white moustache, who holds Jonathan Harker prisoner in his castle and keeps no other servants. He has a strong aquiline face, pale skin, sharp canine teeth and an unnaturally powerful grip, and he speaks proudly of his house's history as if he had lived its battles. He controls wolves with a raised hand and climbs castle walls headfirst like a lizard.
The region of Carpathian mountains that Harker is travelling into, known to him only from books.

Transylvania is a country in eastern Europe, containing a wild mountainous region inside the Carpathians. Its population is split among four peoples: Saxons to the south, Wallachs mixed among them, Magyars to the west, and Szekelys to the east and north, the last said to trace their ancestry to Attila and the Huns.

Transylvania is a country in eastern Europe, a mountainous land inside the Carpathians, divided among Saxons, Wallachs, Magyars and Szekelys. The Count holds that the Szekelys, who he says descend from Attila and the Huns, are a proud and warlike people, and he speaks of the Dracula line as their leaders.

Transylvania is a mountainous land in eastern Europe, inside the Carpathians, divided among Saxons, Wallachs, Magyars and Szekelys. The Count, who speaks as if he were present at its battles, describes the Szekelys as a proud, warlike people descended from Attila and the Huns, with the Dracula line among their leaders.

Transylvania is a mountainous region in eastern Europe, set within the Carpathians and divided among Saxons, Wallachs, Magyars and Szekelys. The Count, speaking as one who has lived its battles, describes the Szekelys as a proud, warlike people said to be descended from Attila and the Huns, with the Dracula line among their leaders. Dracula's homeland, the Count's castle, is somewhere in its wild east.
A legendary conqueror of the Huns whose blood Dracula claims flows in his veins.

Attila is a legendary ancestral figure, the Hun leader from whom the Szekelys are said to descend. The Count, a Szekely nobleman, calls him a blood-relation of his own line and boasts of him as a warrior greater than any devil or witch.
Dracula's people, a proud race of warriors whose blood and history he claims as his own.

The Szekelys are a people of eastern and northern Transylvania, who claim descent from Attila and the Huns. Count Dracula speaks of his own race as Szekelys, proud of their warlike past and of their role guarding frontiers. They are described as a fierce, conquering nation, and the Count sees himself as part of their blood.

Slovaks are a people of the Carpathian region, met by the narrator on his journey through the countryside near Bistritz and the Borgo Pass. They are described as wild-looking, with big cowboy-style hats, baggy white trousers, studded leather belts, high boots, long black hair and heavy moustaches. They are said to be harmless and rather lacking in self-assertion, and they travel on peasant carts carrying long staves.

Slovaks are a wild-looking people of the Carpathian region, with wide hats, nail-studded belts, dirty sheepskins, high boots and long black hair and moustaches. The narrator is told they are harmless and lacking in self-assertion, though they seem barbarian to him. They drive the leiter-wagons that carry the Count's boxes of earth, and they hold long staves and obey the Szgany's orders.

Slovaks are a wild-looking people of the Carpathian region, with wide hats, nail-studded belts, dirty sheepskins, high boots, long black hair and heavy moustaches. The narrator finds them more barbarian than the others he sees, and is told they are harmless and lacking in self-assertion. They drive the leiter-wagons that carry the Count's boxes of earth, handle the crates with ease, and carry long staves; some are said to trade goods down the river to the port.
A mountain pass in the Carpathians through which the coach travels and where Harker expects Dracula's carriage.

Borgo Pass is a mountain pass in the Carpathians, leading from the frontier town of Bistritz into Bukovina. At night it is dark, steep and eerie, and the coach's passengers grow visibly agitated as they enter it. Locals make protective gestures and press small gifts on the traveller, and the pass is where a carriage was supposed to meet him.

Borgo Pass is a mountain pass in the Carpathians, opening from the frontier town of Bistritz into Bukovina. It is dark, steep and eerie at night, and the coach's passengers grow agitated as they enter it, pressing gifts and making protective signs. Count Dracula's carriage was arranged to meet the traveller there, but no vehicle is waiting when the coach arrives.

Borgo Pass is a mountain pass in the Carpathians, leading from the frontier town of Bistritz into Bukovina. It is steep, shadowed and eerie at dusk and night, and passengers grow agitated as they enter it, offering protective gifts and signs. Count Dracula's carriage was meant to meet travellers there, but none waits on the arrival of the coach. Later the pass is reached by a party that stops at dawn to hypnotise Mina Harker, who then points out the road onward.
An old-fashioned hotel in Bistritz where Harker stays and where the landlady gives him a crucifix.

An English traveller and diarist who keeps a shorthand journal on his trip into the Carpathians. He is methodical, curious about local customs, and a faithful Churchman who is uneasy about superstition.
Has just been made a full solicitor after passing his examinations, and fears the strange journey he has embarked upon.
Has been seriously ill with brain fever and is being nursed at a hospital in Buda-Pesth.
Gravely ill and much weakened, with the resolution gone from his eyes, and he has lost memory of recent events.
Has married Mina in Buda-Pesth and has asked her never to learn the secret recorded in his note-book.
Says he believes the Count is in London and that Van Helsing is the man to unmask and hunt him.
Is travelling to Whitby and then London to trace the consignment of fifty boxes of earth to its London location.
Has kept the vampire-hunting details from Mina and plans to trace the earth-boxes through local inquiries.
Mina's husband, who is dazed and then roused from a drugged stupor, and who says he will hunt the Count.

Jonathan Harker is an English traveller arriving at Bistritz, the frontier town near the Borgo Pass, where he is expected at the Golden Krone Hotel. He is a curious, observant visitor who wants to see the local customs, and he introduces himself to the hotel's staff. He is awaiting a carriage to take him onward to a host who has written to welcome him.

Prisoner in Count Dracula's castle, having resolved to hide his fears and his knowledge of his captivity from the Count. An English solicitor, newly qualified, who keeps a journal, is curious and observant about local customs, and polite in manner, though uneasy about the strange path he has taken. He works on the Count's business with Peter Hawkins, the Exeter lawyer.

Jonathan Harker is an English solicitor, newly qualified, who keeps a careful journal and records what he sees with curiosity and courtesy. He is polite and observant about local customs but uneasy about the strange journey he has undertaken. He works on the Count's property and legal business alongside Peter Hawkins, the Exeter lawyer.

An English solicitor, newly qualified, who keeps a careful journal and notes what he sees with curiosity and courtesy. He is polite about local customs but uneasy about his strange journey. He works on the Count's property and legal business with Peter Hawkins, the Exeter lawyer, and is engaged to Mina Murray, who writes of him with affection and worry; he has sent no word for some time.

Newly qualified English solicitor who keeps a careful shorthand journal and travels abroad on legal business for Peter Hawkins of Exeter. Engaged to Mina Murray, and she is set to join him at a Buda-Pesth hospital, where he is nursed by Sister Agatha after a grave illness that has left him weakened and without memory of recent events.

Jonathan Harker is a newly qualified English solicitor who keeps a journal and is engaged to Mina Murray; he has been gravely ill and nursed in a hospital in Buda-Pesth. He is much weakened, has lost memory of recent events, and has married Mina, asking her never to learn the secret in his note-book. He is said to believe the Count is in London, and he travels on legal business to trace fifty boxes of earth.

Jonathan Harker is a young English solicitor who keeps a journal and was once gravely ill, nursed in a hospital in Buda-Pesth. He married Mina Murray there and became a partner in Mr. Hawkins's firm. He suffers lapses of memory and dizziness, and his sealed foreign journal is kept from Mina's reading at his request.

Peter Hawkins is a solicitor of Exeter, a man the Count calls his friend and to whom Jonathan Harker is connected through legal work. He sends a letter vouching for a substitute agent, and his papers and purchase arrangements pass through Harker. He is absent from the scene itself, referred to rather than present.

Peter Hawkins is a solicitor of Exeter, working at a distance from London and the Count's affairs. The Count calls him his friend and treats him as the agent who arranges the London estate purchase, with papers passing through Jonathan Harker. Harker is to work with him on legal matters in Exeter. Hawkins is never present in the scenes, only referred to.

Peter Hawkins is a solicitor of Exeter, far from London, who acts as agent for Count Dracula's London estate purchase, with Jonathan Harker working for him on legal papers. The Count calls him his friend. Mina Murray, who corresponds with him, regards him as kind, and he passes on letters from Harker.

Dead: Peter Hawkins, the Exeter solicitor, died suddenly and was to be buried in his father's grave. He is an elderly, kind man of Exeter, senior partner of the firm Hawkins & Harker, to which Jonathan Harker was made partner. He acted as agent for Count Dracula's London estate purchase and was a friend of the Count. He was like a father to Jonathan Harker and Mina Murray, who regarded him with great affection, and he left them his fortune.

Purfleet is a place rather than a character: a locality on a by-road, where an estate called Carfax is for sale. It is walled in, with an old oak-and-iron gate. Nearby stands a large house recently turned into a private lunatic asylum.

Purfleet is a locality on a by-road, where an old walled estate called Carfax is for sale, with a rusted oak-and-iron gate. Nearby stands a large house recently turned into a private lunatic asylum. Harker and his friends go there for their business, and Mina is at home there with the others, so it also serves as their base at one point.
A house near Purfleet, currently empty, to which the consignment of fifty boxes is ordered delivered.
The old house near Seward's asylum where the boxes of earth were kept and where the men now sterilise them.

Carfax is an old estate near Purfleet, with a high wall, a large, straggling house and an ancient chapel, and a dark pond among its trees. Its name is said to be a corruption of an old phrase, since the house is four-sided. The house stands empty and for sale, and it is ordered that a consignment of fifty boxes be placed in its ruined chapel.

Carfax is an old, walled estate near Purfleet: a large, straggling, four-sided house with a thick stone keep-like section, an ancient chapel, a dark pond and many trees. It stands empty and for sale, and is the place where fifty boxes are ordered to be delivered and deposited in its ruined chapel. A telegram is addressed to Seward at Carfax, though it is delivered late.

An old, walled estate near Purfleet, four-sided and straggling, with a thick stone keep-like section, an ancient chapel, a dark pond and many trees. It stands empty and for sale, and is where fifty boxes of earth are ordered deposited in the ruined chapel. A telegram is addressed to Seward at Carfax but is delivered late.

A walled, old estate near Purfleet, four-sided and largely empty, with a thick stone keep-like section and an ancient chapel. It is where fifty boxes of earth are ordered deposited, and a telegram is addressed to Seward there.

A walled, old estate near Purfleet, four-sided and largely overgrown, with a thick stone keep-like section and an ancient chapel. It is the house where the fifty earth-filled boxes were ordered deposited, and a related telegram is addressed to Seward there. Its own grounds are said to be gloomy, with a dark pond and a stream.
A harbour town with a pier, a lighthouse, an East Cliff churchyard and a steep stone abbey steps leading up from the harbour.

Whitby is a place on the Yorkshire coast, marked with a small ring in an atlas that Jonathan Harker finds in Count Dracula's library. It is also the address of Samuel F. Billington, to whom the Count's letter is directed at No. 7, The Crescent.

Whitby is a seaside town on the Yorkshire coast, a place with a steep river valley, a harbour, red-roofed old streets and a ruined abbey above them. In an atlas in Count Dracula's library it is marked with a small ring. Samuel F. Billington lives there at No. 7, The Crescent, the address on one of the Count's letters, and Mina Murray visits there, where Lucy Westenra is staying.

A seaside town on the Yorkshire coast, set in a steep river valley above a harbour with two piers and lighthouses. Its red-roofed old streets rise beneath a ruined abbey, and its East Cliff churchyard, crowded with tombstones, overlooks the harbour and the bay; townsfolk gather there to watch the sea and weather.

A harbour town on the Yorkshire coast, with a steep river valley, red-roofed old streets and a ruined abbey rising above the town. Its East Cliff churchyard, crowded with tombstones, overlooks the harbour, piers and lighthouses and the bay beyond. Storms here can rise suddenly, and the harbour takes in damaged vessels.
A legendary leader in Dracula's account of the Hungarian conquest, remembered in the Count's story of his race.

Buda-Pesth is a city on the Danube that the narrator sees briefly from a train and on a short walk near the station. He finds it wonderful and feels he is passing from the West into the East. Its letter addressee, a bank of Klopstock & Billreuth, is where the Count sends mail.

Buda-Pesth is a city on the Danube, reached by train from Vienna, which the narrator finds wonderful and feels as a passage from West to East. It is home to the bankers Klopstock & Billreuth, to whom the Count addresses a letter, and it houses a hospital of St. Joseph and Ste. Mary, where Sister Agatha works and where Jonathan is said to be ill.
A London bank that receives one of Dracula's letters.
A man at Varna who receives one of Dracula's letters, known to Harker only from the envelope.
Herr Leutner is the recipient of a letter that Count Dracula writes and seals, addressed to a man at Varna. Nothing else in these passages says who or what he is.
Bankers at Buda-Pesth who receive one of Dracula's unsealed letters.

Samuel F. Billington is a Whitby solicitor with offices at 7, The Crescent, to whom a cargo of wooden boxes is consigned. He is also an addressee of a letter that Dracula, the Count, has written and left sealed for posting, and he goes aboard the schooner Demeter to take formal possession of the goods.

A Whitby solicitor with offices at 7, The Crescent, who appears as the consignee of the Demeter's cargo of wooden boxes and formally takes possession of those goods. He is also an addressee of a letter the Count leaves sealed for posting. Later passages show him trading as Samuel F. Billington & Son, a firm that writes to Messrs. Carter, Paterson & Co. in London urging speed.
The Russian port from which the Demeter sailed.
Varna is a port city, the place a Russian schooner sailed from before reaching Whitby. It is also the address of a man, Herr Leutner, to whom a letter is sent. Nothing more is shown of it.
Varna is a port city on the Black Sea, from which a Russian schooner, the Demeter, is said to have sailed to Whitby. It is also the place where Herr Leutner, a recipient of letters, has his address.

Varna is a Black Sea port city. Ships bound for it leave England, and the passages say it is where the Demeter came from and where the boxes were to be landed. A letter-recipient, Herr Leutner, has his address there.

Varna is a Black Sea port city, the place where the Demeter set out and the Czarina Catherine sailed from. The boxes from the Demeter were to be landed there for an agent named Ristics, and Herr Leutner has his address there. Later, the travellers reach its hotel, the Odessus, to await a ship.
A character from Shakespeare's play, cited by Harker as a reference point for his own unsettled mind.

Hamlet is a figure the narrator mentions only in comparison: a character in Shakespeare whose father's ghost is invoked as a parallel to the diary-writer's broken-off entries, and whose lines the narrator recalls while distressed. Hamlet is not shown acting in these passages, and no ties, rank or fate are stated for him.

A band of gipsies, peculiar to this part of the world, fearless and without religion save superstition, who attach themselves to a noble and speak their own Romany tongue. They are in the Count's service and camp in the castle courtyard.

The Szgany are a band of gipsies, peculiar to this part of the world yet related to gipsies everywhere, and numerous in Hungary and Transylvania. They are said to attach themselves to a great noble or boyar and take his name, and are described as fearless, without religion beyond superstition, and speaking only their own Romany varieties. A band of them works at the castle under a leader called the hetman, and they serve the Count.

The Szgany are a band of gipsies, found in Hungary and Transylvania and related to gipsies elsewhere, who live almost outside the law. They are said to attach themselves to a great noble or boyar and take his name, and are described as fearless and without religion beyond superstition, speaking only their own Romany varieties. A band works at the castle under a leader called the hetman, carrying out heavy tasks there, and they serve the Count, who sends their cargo by river to Slovaks.
Mina's dear friend since childhood, a young woman near twenty who has received several proposals. She has accepted a love she has not yet told in words, and is loved by Arthur.
Has recovered her health and appetite at Whitby and has stopped walking in her sleep; engaged to Arthur.
Relapsed sharply after the first transfusion, showing ghastly pallor and two small punctures on her throat.

Lucy Westenra is a young woman who corresponds with Mina Murray and writes candidly about her romantic life. She is lively and warm, and she is courted by several suitors: Arthur, Dr. Seward and Quincey P. Morris, whom she describes as an American from Texas. She writes of being very happy, having accepted a proposal from one of them.

Young woman who writes frankly to Mina Murray about her romantic life and is courted by several men, including Arthur Holmwood, Dr. Seward and Quincey P. Morris, an American from Texas whose proposal she declines. Lively and sweet with older people, and her colour has grown rosy at Whitby, where she is staying. She walks in her sleep, and her mother asks Mina to lock their door at night.

Young woman engaged to Arthur Holmwood, son of Lord Godalming, and close friend of Mina Murray. Earlier courted by Dr. Seward and by Quincey Morris, whose proposal she declined; she is lively and gentle with older people. Her colour and health have improved at Whitby, though by late August she feels weak, uneasy and troubled by dreams.

Young woman engaged to Arthur Holmwood, son of Lord Godalming, and close friend of Mina Murray. Earlier courted by Quincey Morris and Dr. Seward, and she declined Morris's proposal. Lively and gentle with older people, she has been sleep-walking and has grown pale and weak, with two small wounds on her throat that have not healed.

Dead by the end of the events shown, after a sharp decline following the transfusions. Lucy Westenra is a young woman engaged to Arthur Holmwood, son of Lord Godalming, and close friend of Mina Murray. Earlier she declined Quincey Morris's proposal; she is lively and gentle, once walked in her sleep, and bears two small wounds on her throat.

Dead, buried alongside her mother, according to a telegram received by Mina. Lucy Westenra is a young woman engaged to Arthur Holmwood and a close friend of Mina Murray. Earlier she declined Quincey Morris's proposal; she is lively and gentle, once walked in her sleep, and bore two small wounds on her throat that did not heal.

Dead, the body staked by Arthur Holmwood as Van Helsing reads the prayers, a death the passages describe in the late chapters. Lucy Westenra is a young woman engaged to Arthur Holmwood and a close friend of Mina Murray. Lively and sweet in manner, she has walked in her sleep, grown pale and weak, and bears two small wounds on her throat that stay open.
Lucy's lover, who came to Hillingham in anxiety and gave blood for her transfusion, becoming very weakened.
Grief-stricken and angry at the proposed desecration of Lucy's grave, yet agrees to go with Van Helsing and wait.

Arthur Holmwood, also styled Hon. Arthur, is a young man in Lucy's circle whom she is in love with and who is engaged to her; Quincey P. Morris writes letters to him and he sends telegrams back. Lucy describes him as a friend of Mr. Holmwood's household and as someone she tells her secrets to, though he has not yet declared his love in words. He is described as the sort of man Lucy would confide in and as someone whose manner is quiet.

Arthur Holmwood, styled Hon. Arthur, is the only son of Lord Godalming and is engaged to Lucy, who calls him by his first name. He is a quiet, well-regarded young man in Lucy's circle; Quincey P. Morris writes to him and he replies by telegram. Lucy confides in him and loves him, though he has not yet declared his feelings in words, and their marriage is planned for the autumn.

Hon. Arthur Holmwood, son of Lord Godalming, is engaged to Lucy Westenra and is a quiet, well-regarded young man in her circle. He is tall with curly hair, visits the Westenra house often, and is called Arthur by Lucy, who confides in him and loves him though he has not said so in words. Quincey P. Morris writes to him and he answers by telegram. His father's serious illness has kept him away for a time, and the wedding is planned for the autumn.

Hon. Arthur Holmwood, son of Lord Godalming, is engaged to Lucy Westenra and is a quiet, well-liked young man in her circle, tall with curly hair. Lucy confides in him and loves him, though he has not said so in words. He answers Quincey P. Morris by telegram, and he has been kept away at times by his father's serious illness. He came to Hillingham in anxiety, gave blood for Lucy's transfusion, and was left very weakened.

Hon. Arthur Holmwood, son of Lord Godalming, is engaged to Lucy Westenra and is a tall, curly-haired, quiet and well-liked young man in her circle. Lucy confides in him and loves him, though he has not said so in words. He is often kept away by his father's serious illness, came to Hillingham in anxiety, and offered to give his own blood for Lucy's transfusion, which left him very weakened.

Hon. Arthur Holmwood, son of Lord Godalming, is engaged to Lucy Westenra and is a tall, curly-haired, quiet and well-liked young man in her circle. Lucy confides in him and loves him, though he has not said so in words. He is often kept away by his father's serious illness, offered his own blood for Lucy's transfusion and was left very weakened, and is grief-stricken and angry at the proposed desecration of Lucy's grave, yet agrees to go with Van Helsing and wait.

Arthur Holmwood, the son of Lord Godalming, is Lucy Westenra's suitor and is called Arthur by her. He is tall with curly hair, quiet and liked by those around him, and he is a friend of Dr. Seward. He gave blood for Lucy's transfusion and was left badly drained. Lucy's death has left him stricken with grief, and he is angry at the planned disturbance of her grave, yet he agrees to go with Van Helsing and wait.

Mr. Holmwood, the Hon. Arthur Holmwood, is the only son of Lord Godalming and a suitor of Lucy's. He is a tall, curly-haired gentleman who visits Lucy's household often and gets on well with her mother. He is expected at Whitby but is often delayed by his father's illness, and Lucy is eager to see him.

A gentleman who is the only son of Lord Godalming, and a suitor courting Lucy. He is tall with curly hair, calls often at her household, and talks easily with her mother. He is due to visit Whitby but keeps being held up by his father's grave illness, which leaves Lucy impatient to see him.
A doctor of twenty-nine who runs a large lunatic asylum. Outwardly calm and resolute, he proposes marriage to Lucy and is refused, and keeps a phonograph diary.
Is a physician who has been asked by Arthur to examine Lucy and who has summoned Van Helsing for help.
Gave his own blood in a second transfusion for Lucy and keeps watch over her with Van Helsing.
Was attacked by Renfield with a dinner-knife and wounded in the left wrist, and has been losing blood and feeling exhausted.
Has been losing blood from a wrist wound and is exhausted, while keeping watch over Lucy with Van Helsing.
Is reluctant to let Mina read his phonograph diary, fearing its account of Lucy's death.
Takes part in the council and simply nods his assent to the pledge against the vampire.
Judges that an inquest would never accept the truth, so he will certify Renfield's death as a fall from bed.

Dr. John Seward is a doctor who runs a lunatic asylum, with a strong jaw and a good forehead. He is nervous and earnest in manner, and he proposes marriage to Lucy Westenra, who turns him down. He is a close friend of Arthur and of Quincey P. Morris.

A physician who runs a lunatic asylum, with a strong jaw and a good forehead. Nervous and earnest in manner, he once proposed marriage to Lucy Westenra, who refused him. A close friend of Arthur Holmwood and Quincey P. Morris. He keeps a diary, examines Lucy for an unexplained weakness, and has summoned Van Helsing to help. He also attends the patient Renfield.

Physician who runs a lunatic asylum, with a strong jaw and a good forehead; nervous and earnest in manner. Wounded in the left wrist by his patient Renfield with a dinner-knife, and has been losing blood and feeling exhausted. He once proposed to Lucy Westenra, who refused him; a close friend of Arthur Holmwood and Quincey P. Morris. He keeps a diary, summoned Van Helsing to help with Lucy, and gave his own blood for her transfusion.

Physician who runs a lunatic asylum and keeps a diary, with a strong jaw and a good forehead; nervous and earnest in manner. Lucy Westenra has died, and Seward led the grieving Arthur away. He once proposed to Lucy, who refused him, and is a close friend of Arthur Holmwood and Quincey P. Morris. He summoned Van Helsing to help with Lucy and gave his own blood for her transfusion. He was wounded in the left wrist by his patient Renfield with a dinner-knife and has been losing blood and feeling exhausted.

Physician who runs a lunatic asylum and keeps a diary, with a strong jaw and good forehead; nervous, earnest and loyal in manner. Once proposed to Lucy Westenra, who refused him, and is a close friend of Arthur Holmwood and Quincey P. Morris. Works alongside Abraham Van Helsing, who told him that Lucy is Un-Dead and asked him to see the proof. Gave his own blood for Lucy's transfusions and was cut in the left wrist by his patient Renfield with a dinner-knife, leaving him drained and exhausted.

A physician who keeps a diary and runs a lunatic asylum, and a close friend of Arthur Holmwood and Quincey P. Morris. He once proposed to Lucy Westenra and works alongside Abraham Van Helsing, who calls him John. He is earnest, loyal and anxious, and he gave his own blood in Lucy's transfusions; he has been weakened by a wrist wound from his patient Renfield, and is exhausted and reluctant to let Mina read his phonograph diary.

Alive, a physician who runs the asylum and keeps a diary, and who has agreed to certify the death of his patient Renfield as a fall from bed, since he judges an inquest would never accept the truth. He is a close friend of Arthur Holmwood and Quincey P. Morris and works alongside Abraham Van Helsing, who calls him John. He is earnest, loyal and anxious, and he gave his own blood in Lucy's transfusions.

Alive, a physician who runs the asylum and keeps a diary, and who has agreed to certify the death of his patient Renfield as a fall from bed, since he judges an inquest would never accept the truth. He is a close friend of Arthur Holmwood and Quincey P. Morris and works alongside Abraham Van Helsing, who calls him John. He is earnest, loyal and anxious; he gave his own blood in Lucy's transfusions and was wounded in the left wrist by Renfield with a dinner-knife, leaving him drained. He takes part in the council against the vampire.
An American from Texas who speaks slang to amuse Lucy but is well educated. He proposes to Lucy, is refused, and remains a loyal friend.
Gives his blood for Lucy's transfusion and says he will follow the instructions of Van Helsing and Seward.
Advises against conspicuous carriages, favouring cabs to avoid attracting attention.
Takes charge of tactical positioning and organises the plan of attack against the Count.

Quincey P. Morris is an American from Texas, a well-educated, jolly and brave man of striking youthful looks and manners. He enjoys telling tales of adventures and, though he sometimes uses American slang when speaking to someone he knows, he is otherwise courteous. He is a close friend of Arthur Holmwood and of Jack Seward, and he proposed to Lucy, who gently refused him because she loves another man.

An American from Texas, young-looking, well educated and courteous, though he sometimes plays with slang among friends. Brave and jolly, a close friend of Arthur Holmwood and Jack Seward, and a former suitor of Lucy, who refused him for another man. He gives his blood for Lucy's transfusion, agrees to follow the instructions of Van Helsing and Seward, and keeps watch around the house at night.

An American from Texas, young-looking and well educated, with courtly manners, though he likes to tease with slang among friends. Brave, jolly and loyal, a close friend of Arthur Holmwood and Jack Seward, and a former suitor of Lucy who accepted her choice of another man. He gives his blood for Lucy's transfusion, agrees to follow the instructions of Van Helsing and Seward, and keeps watch around the house at night.

An American from Texas, young-looking and courteous, who is well educated and jokes in slang when speaking to friends. He is a close friend of Arthur Holmwood and Jack Seward and once loved Lucy, wanting to marry her. He gives his blood for Lucy's transfusion, patrols the house at night, and goes with the group to the tomb, where he helps hold Arthur steady during the staking. He is steady and brave, and Seward admires him.

Mortally wounded in the side and dying, with his life ebbing away. Quincey P. Morris is an American from Texas, young-looking, courteous and well educated, and a close friend of Arthur Holmwood and Jack Seward, who once loved Lucy. He is steady and brave, gave blood for Lucy's transfusion, patrolled the house at night, and took charge of tactical positioning.
A patient at Dr. Seward's asylum, aged fifty-nine, with a sanguine temperament and great physical strength, morbidly excitable and prone to fixed ideas.
Keeps a notebook of figures and collects flies and spiders, reasoning that absorbing life is strength; Seward calls him a zoophagous maniac.
Ate the sparrows he had tamed, and is now a homicidal maniac craving a cat to kill.

A patient at Dr. Seward's asylum, aged fifty-nine, with a sanguine temperament and great physical strength. Obsessed with collecting and consuming living things, he is a homicidal maniac whom Seward studies with clinical fascination.
Calms with the moon, then turns violent by day; he claims the attendants think he could hurt Seward, and he collects flies.
A patient of Dr. Seward who swallows insects and alternates between violent fits and sudden lucidity. He pleads to be released, insisting his sanity and a duty that binds him.

R. M. Renfield is a patient in Dr. Seward's asylum, a man of about fifty-nine with great physical strength and a sanguine but morbidly excitable temperament. He keeps a habit of swallowing flies and spiders, and once believed that consuming living things and blood could prolong his own life. By turns gloomy and then courtly and articulate, he can speak with the polish of a gentleman, though he is considered possibly dangerous.

R. M. Renfield is a patient in Dr. Seward's asylum, a man of about fifty-nine with great physical strength and a sanguine, morbidly excitable temperament. He keeps a habit of swallowing flies and spiders, and once believed that consuming living things and blood could prolong life. By turns gloomy and then courtly and articulate, he speaks with the polish of a gentleman, yet he is considered possibly dangerous and once attacked Seward.

Dead, his neck broken on the floor, as the attendant reports hearing voices and Renfield crying out to God. A patient in Dr. Seward's asylum, a man of about fifty-nine with great physical strength and a sanguine, morbidly excitable temperament. He once believed that consuming living things, even blood, could prolong life; by turns gloomy, then courtly and articulate with the polish of a gentleman, yet considered possibly dangerous and once attacked Seward.
A headland stretching out into the sea beyond Whitby's bay, where a man fell from the rocks.

Kettleness is a headland that juts out into the sea beyond Whitby's harbour, seen from the churchyard above the town. It is a steep, grey cliff-point, and the passages mention a tombstone at its edge recording a man's fatal fall there.

Kettleness is a steep headland jutting into the sea up the bay from Whitby's harbour, visible from the churchyard above the town. It is a dark, grey cliff-point, lying beyond the harbour's lighthouses, and at its edge a tombstone records a man's fall from the rocks there. Its black mass also stands against the western sky at sunset.
A large ruined abbey above the town, said to have a white lady seen in one of its windows.
A very old former Greenland whaling sailor, nearly a hundred, with a gnarled face and a blunt, sceptical manner. He mocks local ghost tales and tombstone inscriptions.
Found dead on the seat in the churchyard with a broken neck and a look of fear, apparently after being frightened.

Mr. Swales is an elderly, talkative local of the Whitby coast, with a thick dialect and a sharp, mocking humour about gravestones and the dead. He is a former sailor who knew many of the drowned men buried in the churchyard, and he gathers with cronies to enjoy his bluntness. Later he turns gentle and approaches the narrator with a quiet, kindly manner.

Dead: found on the seat in the churchyard with a broken neck and a look of fear, apparently after being frightened. A former sailor from the Whitby coast, he was an elderly, talkative local with a thick dialect and a mocking humour about gravestones and the drowned, having known many of the men buried there. Latterly he had grown gentle and kindly toward the narrator.
A master mariner commemorated on a Whitby gravestone as murdered by pirates; the body is not buried there, according to Mr. Swales.
A man buried in the churchyard whose gravestone Mr. Swales says is false; he died falling from the rocks at Kettleness.

George Canon is a dead man, named on a gravestone at Kettleness, said to have fallen from the rocks there in 1873. Per local Mr. Swales, he was a disabled son who hated his mother, and his death was a suicide rather than an accident; these are Swales's claims, not confirmed facts.

Geordie is a figure in the local talk of Whitby's churchyard, invoked by the old man Swales as someone who climbs the steps carrying a gravestone on his back. He is a lively, mocking presence in Swales's jokes, not a person the narrator has met. Geordie is not described beyond that.
Joins the pledge against the vampire for Lucy's sake and holds Van Helsing's hand in the compact.

Lord Godalming is the father of Arthur Holmwood, and is described as a close friend of Mrs. Westenra. He is not in good health, and is said to have been taken seriously ill, which calls his son away. He is mentioned only through others and does not appear directly in these passages.

Lord Godalming is the father of Arthur Holmwood, the Hon. Arthur Holmwood, and a dear friend of Mrs. Westenra. He is a sick, elderly man whose serious illness calls his son away, and he is referred to only through others, never appearing directly. A solicitor's remark that he would have had no claim on the estate suggests he was not a relative of Mrs. Westenra's family. In a letter, Van Helsing says that Lord Godalming has given him access to Lucy's letters and papers.

Lord Godalming is the father of the Hon. Arthur Holmwood, who is his only son, and a close friend of Mrs. Westenra. He is an elderly man in poor health, so his illness keeps Arthur away and he is spoken of only through others, never appearing directly. A solicitor remarks he would have had no claim on the estate, showing he was not a blood relative of the Westenra family. He has given Van Helsing access to Lucy's letters and papers.

Lord Godalming is the Hon. Arthur Holmwood's father, an elderly man in poor health who is kept at Ring and is seen only through others, never directly. He is a close friend of Mrs. Westenra's family and is said to have no claim on her estate. He has given Van Helsing access to Lucy's letters and papers, and he joins the pact against the vampire for Lucy's sake, holding Van Helsing's hand in the compact.

The Hon. Arthur Holmwood's father, Lord Godalming, is an elderly man in poor health, kept at Ring and seen only through others. He is a close friend of the Westenra family and has no claim on Mrs. Westenra's estate. He lends Van Helsing access to Lucy's papers, and he joins the pact against the vampire for Lucy's sake.

Lord Godalming is an elderly, frail peer, father of the Hon. Arthur Holmwood, and a close friend of the Westenra family. He is said to be ill, and he has no claim to Mrs. Westenra's estate. He lends his authority to Van Helsing's access to Lucy's papers, and he joins the pledge against the vampire for Lucy's sake, clasping hands in the compact. He is a loyal, courteous man, and he is practical in action, quick to free the dogs and bolt the great door in the vault and to press on with the search.
A cliff at Whitby with a churchyard and a new searchlight, from which people watch the sea.

East Cliff is a high headland overlooking Whitby harbour, with a churchyard along its top from which townspeople watch the sea. It is a commanding lookout where the searchlight is set up, and it is the place near Tate Hill Pier where the wrecked schooner runs aground and a large dog leaps ashore and vanishes toward the cliff.

East Cliff is a headland above Whitby harbour, with an old churchyard on its top, near St. Mary's Church and the abbey ruins. Townspeople gather there to watch the sea, and a favourite bench overlooks the harbour. It is a lookout where a searchlight is set up, and it lies across the harbour from the West Cliff.
A steamer making trips up and down the coast from Whitby.
A place near Whitby visited by holiday-makers.

Mulgrave Woods is a place near Whitby, reached by road or by the cliff-path, where holiday-makers go on trips. Lucy and the narrator take a picnic lunch there one fine day, with Mrs. Westenra driving them by road. It is a woodland spot the characters visit for pleasure.
A bay near Whitby visited by holiday-makers.
A coastal place near Whitby visited on day trips.
A steamer making trips up and down the coast from Whitby.
A coastal place near Whitby visited on day trips.
A pier in Whitby harbour, where the Demeter comes to rest on a sand heap.

Tate Hill Pier is a small pier in Whitby harbour, a rough accumulation of sand and gravel at the south-east corner of the harbour, lying under the East Cliff. Its homes are close by, and it is a landing place where a schooner can run aground and where a crowd gathers to watch. It also serves as the route bearing a coffin from its landing up the abbey steps to the churchyard.
A figure of steadfast duty invoked by the correspondent as a comparison for the dead steersman who held his post until death.
A doctor of 33 East Elliot Place who examined the dead steersman of the derelict Demeter and judged he had been dead about two days.
The official body whose inspectors exact compliance with regulations for the derelict ship at Whitby.

The Board of Trade is an official body whose inspectors oversee ships and their paperwork in Whitby. They are exacting and thorough, insisting that every regulation is followed, and they grant the narrator access to a ship's log-book.
A Russian schooner from Varna, carrying silver sand and boxes of earth, that drove into Whitby harbour in a storm with a dead man lashed to its wheel.

Demeter is a Russian schooner out of Varna, carrying a cargo of wooden boxes of mould and ballast of silver sand. It is found wrecked in a storm at Whitby, and its log and a message in a bottle are examined at an inquest.
The consul who acts for the charter-party, takes formal possession of the ship and pays its harbour dues.

The Russian consul is an official acting for the charter-party of the Russian schooner Demeter at Whitby, where he takes formal possession of the ship and pays its harbour dues. He has a clerk who translates for the narrator, and he is a man of official duty rather than personal depth in these passages.
The animal welfare society that is strong in Whitby and tries to befriend the dog.
A strait the Demeter passes through on its voyage, where Turkish customs officers board the ship.

Bosphorus is a strait the ship passes through, where Turkish Customs officers board and inspect the vessel and its cargo. The passages treat it as a waterway on a sea route, with no further character or standing attached to it.
A strait the Demeter passes through, where more customs officers board.

Dardanelles is a strait on the route ships take from the Bosphorus into the Archipelago, where Customs officers board vessels and a guarding squadron's flagboat is present. It is also the point the Czarina Catherine is expected to pass, so the travellers await reports from there.
A headland the Demeter passes in the Archipelago.
A crewman of the Demeter who relieves Petrofsky on watch.
A crewman of the Demeter who vanished from his watch.
A crewman of the Demeter who reported seeing a tall, thin stranger come up the companion-way.
A London carrying firm that handled the delivery of fifty boxes to Carfax and returned an overplus cheque.

Carter, Paterson & Co. is a London firm that deals in business correspondence and deliveries. It is written to by Samuel F. Billington & Son of Whitby, a solicitors' firm, and replies through a clerk who signs for the company. Its letters are formal and businesslike, reporting that goods were delivered as instructed and returning an overpayment.
A London goods station where the consignment is to be received and collected.

names.value: Hospital of St. Joseph and Ste. Mary

facets.text: The hospital in Buda-Pesth where Jonathan Harker is being nursed.

Sister Agatha is a nurse at the Hospital of St. Joseph and Ste. Mary in Buda-Pesth, where she cares for Jonathan Harker after he falls ill with brain fever. She writes with warmth and sympathy, speaking for Harker while he is too weak to write himself, and she acts as a caretaker who wants others in need to be helped too.

A nurse and sister at the Hospital of St. Joseph and Ste. Mary in Buda-Pesth, where she tends Jonathan Harker through a severe brain fever. She writes warmly and with sympathy, dictating letters on his behalf while he is too weak to write, and she wishes to see his payment used to help others in need. Her patients' ravings are, in her view, a confidence she will not break, and she is described as a sweet, good woman and a born nurse.
A station from which Jonathan arrived at Buda-Pesth by train, shouting for a ticket home.
A figure quoted by Dr. Seward for a remark about life, cited as someone who knew life well.

Hillingham is the house where Lucy Westenra lives with her mother, Mrs. Westenra. It is a home in town that Lucy has returned to, and it is where Arthur comes for lunch and tea and where Dr. Jack Seward visits to examine Lucy, with Van Helsing also called in.

Hillingham is the town house where Lucy Westenra lives with her mother, Mrs. Westenra, and it is where Lucy has returned after a stay away. Arthur comes there for lunch and tea, and Dr. Jack Seward and Van Helsing visit to examine Lucy and sit with her through the night.

Amsterdam is a city, the home of Professor Van Helsing, an elderly physician and scholar whom John Seward praises as a learned man of wide views and great resolve. Seward writes to him for help with Lucy Westenra, and Van Helsing travels from Amsterdam to London to examine her.

Amsterdam is a city, and the home of Professor Van Helsing, an elderly physician and scholar. John Seward writes to Van Helsing there for help with Lucy Westenra, and Van Helsing travels from it to London to examine her. Van Helsing repeatedly returns to Amsterdam, and telegrams to him are sent there.

Amsterdam is a city and the home of Professor Van Helsing, an elderly physician and scholar of obscure diseases. Van Helsing travels from it to London and back, and telegrams to him are sent there. Seward writes to him there for help.
A London railway station where Seward meets Van Helsing on arrival.

Liverpool Street is a London railway station where Van Helsing meets Dr. Seward at the start of the passages, and Van Helsing later drives there to leave. It is a place, not a person, and the passages show nothing further about its nature.
A mythical river of forgetting, mentioned by Van Helsing when describing the garlic's effect.
A town from which Van Helsing's garlic flowers were sent, grown in the glass-houses of his friend Vanderpool.

Haarlem is a town, not a person, and is where the garlic flowers come from: Van Helsing has them sent from there by a friend, Vanderpool, who grows herbs in his glass-houses. Lucy receives a boxful from Haarlem every day, and it is described as a source of comfort to her.
A friend of Van Helsing who grows herbs in glass-houses at Haarlem.
A newspaper whose interviewer seeks out the zoo keeper for a story about the escaped wolf.

The Pall Mall Gazette is a newspaper whose name a reporter uses as a password to get people to talk. In these passages it runs a feature on an escaped wolf, with an interviewer who visits the zoo keeper Thomas Bilder at his cottage. It is shown only as a publication and a name opening doors, not as a character with traits of its own.
An elderly, talkative keeper at the Zoological Gardens who speaks in thick dialect, enjoys a joke, and cares for the wolves.

Thomas Bilder is the keeper in the wolf section of the Zoölogical Gardens, living in a cottage behind the elephant-house with his wife. He is elderly, hospitable and talkative, given to folksy, teasing talk and confident opinions about wolves. He takes the escaped wolf Bersicker back in with tender care.
A grey wolf kept at the Zoological Gardens, well-behaved until he escapes his cage and later returns, docile and penitent.

Bersicker is a grey wolf, one of three from Norway bought by Jamrach's menagerie, kept by the keeper Bilder. Described as a well-behaved animal that rarely caused trouble, it breaks out of its cage one night, and is later said to be a dangerous 'wicked wolf'. It is quick, and takes to a strange thin man in white gloves who strokes its ears.
A dealer from whom the zoo bought three grey wolves from Norway four years earlier.
A solicitor of the firm handling Mrs. Westenra's affairs, genial and appreciative, who explains the will.
The firm of solicitors to which Mrs. Westenra's affairs were entrusted.
A park near Arlington Street from which Van Helsing and Seward watch the Piccadilly house.

Green Park is a shaded public park in London, where the travellers sit to rest and where they wait within sight of a house. It serves as a quiet, comfortable place to pause and watch, and the passages show it only as a setting for these moments.

Hampstead is a place: a hill and heath north of London, with a churchyard nearby where Lucy lies in her family tomb, its air fresh and its flowers wild. In the newspaper reports it is a neighbourhood where young children have been going missing on the Heath, several found weak and marked with small throat wounds.

The Westminster Gazette is a newspaper that prints reports of local events, appearing in the passages as a printed source with dated issues. It publishes stories on a mysterious series of child disappearances and injuries near Hampstead Heath, including an extra edition. Its reporting presents the children's accounts of being lured away by a so-called 'bloofer lady', which is only what the children are said to claim.

The Westminster Gazette is a London newspaper whose printed issues carry dated reports of local events. It runs stories on a run of child disappearances and throat injuries near Hampstead Heath, including an extra edition, and its reports relay the children's claims of being lured away by a 'bloofer lady'. Characters read it as a source of news, with one reader recognising it by its colour.

Mrs. Harker is a woman who writes letters, telegrams and diary entries in her own voice, and keeps a typewritten record of papers. She is loyal and tender toward Jonathan Harker, careful with his nerves, and quietly resolute about a possible duty. She observes people closely, describing Dr. Van Helsing's strong, resolute face, and she turns to him for help.

Mrs. Harker is Jonathan Harker's wife, a sweet, dainty and tender woman who keeps diaries and letters in her own voice and types out the papers the group gathers. She is careful of her husband's nerves and quietly resolute, and she observes others closely. She is met by Dr. Seward at Paddington and tells Lord Godalming and Mr. Morris how she has ordered the record.

Mrs. Harker, wife of Jonathan Harker, a sweet, dainty and sad-eyed young woman who types out and orders the group's diaries and letters. She is tender and careful of her husband, quick to notice others, and calm and courteous even with Mr. Renfield. Dr. Van Helsing regards her as remarkably capable, with a clever mind and a woman's heart, and wants her kept from the danger ahead.

Wife of Jonathan Harker, a sweet-faced, dainty and sad-eyed young woman who types and arranges the group's diaries, letters and records. She is tender toward her husband, quick to notice others, and calm and courteous even with the unstable Mr. Renfield. Dr. Van Helsing regards her as having a man's brain and a woman's heart, and wants her kept out of the dangerous work.

Wife of Jonathan Harker, a sweet-faced, dainty and sad-eyed young woman. She types and arranges the group's diaries, letters and records, and is tender toward her husband. She is courteous and calm even with Mr. Renfield, quick to notice others, and Dr. Van Helsing regards her as having a man's brain and a woman's heart, wanting her kept out of the dangerous work.

Wife of Jonathan Harker, known to the group as Mina, a sweet-faced, dainty and sad-eyed young woman with a man's brain and a woman's heart. She types and arranges the group's diaries, letters and records, and is courteous, calm and quick to notice others, including the lunatic Renfield. She is tender toward her husband, and Dr. Van Helsing wants her kept out of the dangerous work.

Telegram is a means of sending short written messages, shown here as a series of urgent notes passed between characters. It appears as messages from Arthur Holmwood, Seward, Van Helsing and Mrs. Harker, sent between London, Amsterdam, Antwerp and Sussex. Its content is brief and often reports a patient's condition or summons someone to come quickly.
A London railway station where Van Helsing will arrive by train.
Paddington is a London railway terminus, mentioned only as a destination reached by train from Exeter. It is where Dr. Van Helsing is to arrive for breakfast or lunch with Mina and Jonathan Harker.
A place from which Jonathan's train leaves on his return journey.
A physician whose work on hypnotism Seward accepts; Van Helsing describes him as deceased.
A long-lived figure from scripture cited by Van Helsing as an example of life beyond ordinary limits.
A man said to have lived one hundred and sixty-nine years, cited by Van Helsing.
A physician at the North Hospital, a friend of Van Helsing and a former acquaintance of Seward, who treats the injured child.

Dr. Vincent is a physician at the North Hospital in London and a friend of Van Helsing, who knew him from Amsterdam where they were in class together. He is a calm, practical doctor who examines a sick child and offers ordinary explanations for the punctures on its throat, such as an animal bite or an escaped bat.
An inn on the heights where the men dine before going to the churchyard.
The family vault in the churchyard where Lucy's coffin is kept.
The village whose churchyard holds Lucy's grave.
A London station that Seward and Mina travel to by Underground.

Fenchurch Street is a place in London, reached by the Underground, and it is where a lunatic asylum stands. Mrs. Harker is taken there after the trip from the station, and a house there is later entered by breaking in with a locksmith's help.
A bat that Morris shot at from the window, seen as a creature of the vampire's kind.
A school of learning the Count is said to have attended in life.

Scholomance is a school in the mountains above Lake Hermanstadt, where the devil is said to claim the tenth scholar as his due. Dracula is said to have studied there, learning secrets that some say were dealings with the Evil One.
A consecrated wafer kept in an envelope, held up by Van Helsing against the Count.

A consecrated wafer carried by Van Helsing in an envelope as a weapon against the Count. He handles it with the crucifixes, garlic and lamps, and it drives the Count back when held out to him. It is kept for the most desperate moment and is not to be used lightly.

A consecrated wafer, a portion of the Host, kept in an envelope and carried by Van Helsing as a weapon against the Count. It is held out to drive him back, as when the Count recoils from it in the bedroom, and it burns Mina's forehead when pressed there. The group also lays pieces of it in the Count's earth-filled boxes to sanctify them.
A Mile End New Town address where six earth-boxes from Carfax were deposited.
A Bermondsey address where six earth-boxes from Carfax were deposited.
A reliable workman and responsible mate who recalls carrying boxes from Carfax to their drop-off addresses.

Joseph Smollet is a London carrier and workman, one of two mates of Harris & Sons, Moving and Shipment Company, who hauled heavy wooden boxes from Carfax. He is steady, sensible and practical, with a dog's-eared notebook recording destinations. He keeps a home in Walworth and is the responsible person of the pair, with Thomas Snelling as his assistant.
A rough carter who moved nine boxes from a Piccadilly house with help from an old, strong man.

Sam Bloxam is a rough-spoken London workman, a drinker known to the Walworth lodging-house and to a foreman at a cold-storage building under construction in Poplar. He is said by a cabman to be a man who could tell something useful about a dusty old house. He has carried heavy boxes by horse and cart from a house at Carfax to one in Piccadilly, and he admits to this as a paid, tight-lipped job.
A Walworth court where Corcoran's lodging-house stands.
A Poplar street where a new cold-storage building was being erected.
House agents in Sackville Street who handled the sale of the Piccadilly house.
A late owner of the Piccadilly house, whose executors sold it.
A foreign nobleman who bought the Piccadilly house, paying in notes over the counter.
A dusty, long-empty house near Piccadilly Circus where nine earth-boxes were left.
An asylum where the attendant once saw a young woman harm her own head.
An attendant at Dr. Seward's asylum who finds Renfield injured and is sent away during the operation.
A street near the Piccadilly house where the cab party gets out.
A scholar whose researches Van Helsing has studied about the Count.
A sailing ship bound for Varna and up the Danube, the vessel on which the Count's earth-box is shipped.

A Black Sea-bound cargo ship sailing from Doolittle's Wharf for Varna, the vessel the companions trace Count Dracula's escape to. It is a ship, not a person, and its captain is described only as swearing and reluctant to take on the thin, pale passenger.

A Black Sea-bound cargo ship that sails from Doolittle's Wharf for Varna. It is a ship, not a person, and the passages show only its voyage: a captain who swears and reluctantly takes aboard a thin, pale passenger with a large box, then reports from the Dardanelles and Galatz. The companions track it closely and are told it is still at sea until it is reported entering Galatz.

The Czarina Catherine is a Black Sea-bound cargo ship sailing from Doolittle's Wharf for Varna. It is a vessel, not a person, and its captain is said to swear heavily. The passages show it reported entering Galatz, where its cargo box was handed off.
A London wharf from which the Czarina Catherine sails for the Black Sea.
The shipping register where the company checks departures of all vessels.
An agent at Varna to whom the box is to be delivered, presenting credentials there.
A place where Morris and Harker once faced a wolf pack.
Repeating rifles Morris proposes adding to the company's armament for the journey.

Winchesters are repeating rifles, proposed by Quincey Morris as weapons to add to the group's armament against wolves and evil things. Quincey, who has a faith in them when trouble is about, suggests them, and Van Helsing agrees to take them along on the journey to Varna.

Winchesters are repeating rifles carried as firearms by the group against wolves and other evil things. Quincey Morris proposes them and has faith in them; Van Helsing agrees to take them, and Mr. Morris and Dr. Seward carry them. In the final passage the gypsies are held at bay by Winchesters and by Lord Godalming and Dr. Seward.
The hotel in Varna where the company stays.
A port the Czarina Catherine is reported to have entered, reached by a train route from Varna.

Galatz is a Danube port city, a place rather than a person. Its arrival is reported by telegram as a ship's entry, and the travellers plan to reach it by the next morning's train. A ship carrying a rival party is said to have rushed up to it through fog, where a man is believed to have made arrangements for escape.

Galatz is a Danube river port that the travellers are heading for. It is the place where the ship Czarina Catherine arrives, and a search there is planned. The city serves as a point of arrival and of possible escape, not a person.
The Scottish-speaking skipper of the Czarina Catherine, superstitious and shrewd about cargo.
A London firm whose agents at Galatz are asked to show the party civility.
Agents at Galatz for the London firm of Hapgood, who receive the party courteously.
Crewmen of the Czarina Catherine who wanted the box thrown overboard.
The address of Immanuel Hildesheim's office at Galatz.
A Hebrew businessman at Galatz who received the box before sunrise and paid agents for it.

A Hebrew businessman with an office in Galatz, a man of sharp, sheep-like features who wears a fez and deals in money. He received a box from the ship Czarina Catherine on instruction by letter, cleared it before sunrise and handed it to Petrof Skinsky. He is paid in cash and bargains hard.
The bank at which an English note was cashed for gold.
A Slovak trader who carried the box up the river and was later found murdered.

A Slovak-connected dealer on the Galatz waterfront who handles river traders bound for the port. He receives a box from Immanuel Hildesheim and passes it on, is later found dead outside a churchyard wall with his throat torn, and is described by neighbours and others as a figure of some suspicion and unpopularity.
A river considered as the likely waterway for the box's ascent.

Pruth is a river, one of two candidates considered as the route by which a boxed cargo was carried upstream by boat. It is said to be more easily navigated than the Sereth, and the narrator's theory is that the Slovaks may have ascended it, though this is not confirmed.
A river considered as the likely waterway, joined at Fundu by the Bistritza.

A river in the Carpathian region, the Sereth, joined at Fundu by the Bistritza, which runs toward the Borgo Pass. Read as a likely waterway for a boat carrying a hidden cargo back toward a castle, chosen as the route for the pursuers' steam launch and their search.
A river running up round the Borgo Pass, joining the Sereth at Fundu.

Bistritza is a river in the Carpathian region, a tributary that joins the Sereth at Fundu and runs up toward the Borgo Pass. Its waters are followed by the searchers in their steam launch, who sail up it and later pass into it, and it is said to form a loop close to the Count's castle.
The place where the Bistritza joins the Sereth.

Fundu is a place where the Sereth and the Bistritza rivers meet, a point the travellers reach while pursuing a boat. Its inhabitants know of recent boats passing, and the travellers hear news there of the launch that had gone up the Bistritza.
The town where Mina and Van Helsing hire a carriage to drive to the Borgo Pass.

Veresti is a town where Mina and Van Helsing arrive at noon and from which they set out for the Borgo Pass. It is the place where Van Helsing buys a carriage and horses and where the travellers gather provisions and warm clothing for the journey.

Veresti is a town in the Carpathian foothills where Mina and Van Helsing arrive at noon and buy a carriage, horses and warm provisions before setting out for the Borgo Pass. Van Helsing's purchases include furs and wraps, and the landlady there packs a large basket of food for the journey.
A point on the river that Harker hopes to reach before meeting his companions.
The licence text that opens the free edition of the book, setting out terms for distributing Project Gutenberg works.

events.summary: Harker arrives at the Golden Krone Hotel in Bistritz and receives a letter from Count Dracula welcoming him.
The innkeeper and his wife refuse to speak of Count Dracula or his castle and seem frightened of Harker's inquiries.
The old landlady begs Harker not to travel on St. George's Eve and gives him a crucifix, which he keeps on.
Villagers make warding signs against the evil eye as Harker's coach leaves Bistritz, and fellow passengers offer him charms.
