At the Borgo Pass no carriage is waiting; a strange driver with a calèche arrives and takes Harker's luggage and him onward.
Wolves gather around the carriage and the driver repels them, while blue flames appear at the roadside during the journey.
The driver stops the carriage in the courtyard of a vast ruined castle with no light in its windows.
Count Dracula greets Harker at the castle door and welcomes him in with an unnaturally cold, powerful handshake.
Dracula carries Harker's luggage up to a bedroom prepared for him and a supper is laid out.
Dracula explains through a letter that gout keeps him from travelling, and that a young servant will assist Harker in his affairs.
Dracula asks Harker to help him learn English idiom and to correct his speech, and gives him free run of the castle except locked rooms.
Dracula explains the blue flames as signs of hidden treasure in a land fought over for centuries.
Harker and Dracula go through the papers for the purchase of the Carfax estate at Purfleet, which Dracula signs.
Harker notices that the atlas shows rings marked near London, Exeter and Whitby.
Dracula appears silently in Harker's room while he shaves, and in a rage at the blood from Harker's cut grabs at his throat before seeing the crucifix.
Dracula throws the shaving glass out of the window, smashing it on the courtyard stones.
Harker finds every door locked and realises the castle is a prison from which he cannot escape.
Harker realises he is a prisoner in the castle and resolves to hide his fears and knowledge from Dracula.
Dracula tells Harker the story of his warrior race, speaking as though he had shared in its battles.
Dracula questions Harker about solicitors, agents and consignments, and Harker realises the Count's careful preparations for business in England.
Dracula insists Harker stay another month to serve his needs and tells him to write letters home.
Dracula hands Harker letters and makes clear he will read them, so Harker resolves to write only formal notes.
Harker secretly reads the letters the Count has left on the table, addressed to Billington, Leutner, Coutts & Co. and Klopstock & Billreuth.
Dracula warns Harker never to sleep anywhere in the castle except his own rooms.
Harker places a crucifix over his bed and resolves never to sleep where Dracula is.
Harker sees Dracula climb head-first down the castle wall like a lizard and disappear into the depths below.
Harker finds the locked hall door without its key and explores a neglected suite of old women's rooms.
Harker falls asleep on a couch in the old rooms, ignoring Dracula's warning.
Three pale women appear in the moonlight and gather around the sleeping Harker, who feels both desire and dread.
Dracula bursts in, seizes the fair woman and drives the women off, declaring Harker belongs to him alone.
Dracula throws a moving bag to the women, who vanish through the window with it, and Harker faints.
Harker wakes in his own bed, unsure whether the Count carried him there, and finds his clothes folded oddly and his watch unwound.
Harker finds the door of the room at the top of the stairs forced against its frame, concluding that his terrifying experience was not a dream.
The Count makes Harker write three post-dated letters falsely saying he is leaving, which the Count will hold back and send later.
Harker realises from the dates the Count has chosen that his life has only a short span left.
A band of Szgany arrives at the castle, and Harker speaks with them through his window to try to send letters home.
Harker throws his letters through the bars with a gold piece, and a Szgany man takes them to post.
The Count opens a letter Harker wrote to Peter Hawkins and burns an unsigned letter he finds, forcing Harker to reseal the first.
Harker finds all his paper, notes, letter of credit and travelling clothes gone, leaving him without means to escape.
Slovaks unload heavy empty boxes into the courtyard while Harker's door is locked from outside and they ignore his cries.
Harker watches from a window and sees the Count leave the castle wearing Harker's own clothes and carrying a bag.
Harker is hypnotised by floating moonlit motes until they take the shapes of the three women, and he flees to his room.
A woman in the courtyard demands her child from the Count, and the Count calls wolves that tear her apart.
In the morning Harker resolves to climb along the castle wall into the Count's window to find a way out.
Harker climbs along the wall into the Count's empty room, finds a store of old gold, and goes down to a chapel and vaults.
Harker finds the Count lying in one of fifty earth-filled boxes in the vault, apparently dead yet warm, and flees.
Harker sees the Count leave the castle again in Harker's clothes, and Harker wishes for a weapon but can find none.
The Count announces that Harker will leave the next day, sending him to the Borgo Pass and a coach to Bistritz.
The Count leads Harker to the great door, but when it opens wolves surge in, and Harker begs him to shut it and wait till morning.
Harker hears the Count telling the three women that the night is his and the next night theirs, and the women laugh and withdraw.
At dawn Harker finds the main door bolted again, having been locked after the Count left.
Harker finds the Count gorged with fresh blood in his box and strikes at his face with a shovel, but the Count's gaze stops the blow and the lid closes again.
Harker hears the Szgany and Slovaks arrive, and a sudden gust shuts the stair door, trapping him again in the Count's room.
Harker hears the boxes carried in and nailed shut, and the Count's men leave, locking the castle behind them.
Harker resolves to leave the castle by climbing the wall, taking some gold with him, and to escape to England.
Dr. Seward proposes marriage to Lucy, and when she admits she cares for someone else he gracefully withdraws.
Quincey Morris proposes to Lucy, is refused, and leaves her with a kiss and his friendship.
Lucy receives a third proposal, which she describes only briefly as a confused moment of kissing.
Seward resolves to study Renfield's hallucinations closely and questions him more fully than before.
Mina arrives at Whitby, where Lucy meets her and they stay at the Crescent, and Mina describes the town and abbey.
Mina speaks with old Mr. Swales, who scoffs at ghost legends and tells her that tombstones are full of lies.
Mr. Swales lectures on the lies carved on tombstones, reading several that he says hold no bodies.
Mr. Swales reveals that George Canon's gravestone is false, since he killed himself to thwart his mother's insurance claim.
Lucy tells Mina about her coming marriage to Arthur, and Mina feels heartsick at having had no word from Jonathan for a month.
Mina sits alone on the churchyard cliff, sad that no letter has come from Jonathan.
Seward notices Renfield's fly-collecting and notebook of figures, and that he eats a fly, arguing it gives him life.
Renfield asks for a kitten, and the spiders and flies have been replaced by a colony of tame sparrows.
Seward refuses Renfield a kitten and sees a homicidal look in his face, which he decides to test.
Renfield's sparrows have vanished, leaving feathers and a drop of blood, and Seward orders the attendant to watch him.
Seward drugs Renfield and reads his notebook, concluding he is a zoophagous maniac who would consume many lives, and considers experimenting on him.
Mina receives a short letter from Jonathan dated from Castle Dracula, saying he is starting for home, which troubles her.
Arthur Holmwood is called to Ring because his father has fallen seriously ill, delaying his visit to Lucy.
Still with no news from Jonathan, Mina finds his last letter unlike him, and Lucy searches the room for the key in her sleep.
Mr. Swales confesses his earlier mockery, speaks of his coming death, and blesses Mina before leaving.
The coastguard reports a strange Russian ship sailing erratically as a storm approaches Whitby.
A sudden storm rises over Whitby after a calm, sultry evening, and a foreign schooner is seen with its sails set.
The coastguard and a doctor examine the dead steersman lashed to the wheel of the derelict schooner.
The Demeter's cargo is consigned to Samuel F. Billington, and the Russian consul takes formal possession of the ship.
The dog that leapt from the ship vanishes, and a coal merchant's mastiff is found dead with its throat torn out.
The inquest returns an open verdict, and the captain is given a public funeral in the churchyard.
At the funeral Lucy grows restless, and Mr. Swales is found dead on the seat with a broken neck.
A man's dog refuses to approach its master during the service and is terrified when forced onto a tombstone.
Mina decides to take Lucy on a long walk to Robin Hood's Bay so she will not sleepwalk.
Billington & Son sends Carter, Paterson & Co. instructions to deliver fifty boxes to Carfax, with keys and payment enclosed.
Carter, Paterson & Co. confirm delivery to Carfax exactly as instructed and return the surplus payment.
Lucy recalls the night of her sleepwalking in the churchyard, and her memory of it is vague and dreamlike.
Mina learns that Jonathan has been ill and receives a letter from Sister Agatha, then prepares to leave for him.
Arthur's father recovers and Lucy's marriage to Arthur is set to take place soon.
Lucy's mother confides to Mina that a doctor has told her she has a weak heart and may die within months.
Lucy grows weaker, and her throat wounds from the safety-pin fail to heal.
Sister Agatha warns that Jonathan's delirium was filled with wolves, poison, blood and ghosts, and that he must be kept calm.
Renfield grows haughty and excited, declaring that the Master is at hand.
Renfield escapes through his window and is found at the chapel of Carfax, claiming to serve his Master.
Renfield is overpowered, restrained in a straitjacket and chained in a padded room.
Jonathan Harker and Mina are married in Buda-Pesth, and Mina seals his note-book unopened.
Renfield becomes quiet by moonrise and Seward plans to watch him, but Renfield escapes again.
Renfield is caught at the old chapel and grows calm after following a bat's path into the sky.
Arthur asks Dr. Seward to examine Lucy, who looks worse each day; Mrs. Westenra is privately told her heart is failing.
Seward finds Lucy physically sound but troubled mentally, and sends for Van Helsing.
Van Helsing examines Lucy, finds no functional cause, and says there must be a cause and that he will return if needed.
Renfield sinks into despair saying he has been deserted, then grows happy again, eats flies and asks for more sugar.
Renfield abandons his fly-collecting after a violent fit at sunset, which Seward notes and connects to the sun.
Seward telegraphs Van Helsing that Renfield has taken a terrible turn and urges him to come at once.
Seward meets Van Helsing at Liverpool Street and reports that he has only told Arthur that Van Helsing is coming.
Van Helsing advises Seward to keep his knowledge to himself and to record his observations carefully.
Van Helsing judges Lucy will die without blood and decides a transfusion must be given at once.
Arthur arrives at the house, anxious, and offers to help; Van Helsing decides to use his blood.
Van Helsing gives Lucy a narcotic and performs a blood transfusion using Arthur's blood.
Van Helsing and Seward notice two punctures on Lucy's throat, which they cannot yet explain.
Van Helsing leaves for Amsterdam and orders Seward to watch Lucy all night.
Lucy sleeps peacefully through the night while Seward keeps watch, after she asks him to wake her if she has bad dreams.
Lucy insists Seward rest at Hillingham while she sleeps, and he lies down in the next room.
Van Helsing and Seward find Lucy near death and pale, and Van Helsing decides on a second transfusion using Seward's blood.
Van Helsing gives Lucy a morphia injection after the second transfusion, and her colour returns.
Van Helsing forbids Seward to mention the transfusion to Arthur, fearing it would alarm and make him jealous.
Van Helsing fills Lucy's room with garlic and places a garlic wreath on her neck, saying it will protect her.
Van Helsing says he will sleep well that night, and Seward feels a vague dread.
Mrs. Westenra tells the doctors that Lucy is better and that she herself removed the flowers and opened a window in Lucy's room.
Van Helsing breaks down in despair after learning the flowers were removed, then resolves to act against the forces he believes threaten Lucy.
Seward performs another blood transfusion on Lucy, with Van Helsing directing and then taking over the second round.
Van Helsing tells Mrs. Westenra that the flowers have medicinal value and that he will watch over Lucy the next two nights.
Lucy reports four peaceful days and nights, with her nightmares ceased and Van Helsing going away to Amsterdam for a day.
The wolf Bersicker escapes from the Zoological Gardens, and the keeper and a visitor discuss how it happened.
Bersicker returns to the zoo on his own, injured about the head, and is locked back in his cage.
Renfield attacks Seward with a dinner-knife, cutting his wrist, and is then subdued and taken away while repeating that the blood is the life.
Van Helsing telegraphs Seward urgently to be at Hillingham that night and to keep the flowers in place, but the telegram arrives twenty-two hours late.
Lucy's mother comes to sleep beside her, and a wolf breaks through the window, causing Mrs. Westenra to die of fright.
Lucy wakes to find the maids drugged with laudanum, and her mother's body lying on the bed beside her.
Lucy writes a memorandum to be found, believing she is dying, and bids farewell to Arthur.
Seward arrives at Hillingham to find the house silent and the doors locked, and he fears Lucy is dead.
Van Helsing and Seward cut through the bars of a kitchen window and enter the house, finding the servants drugged and Lucy and her mother lying in the bedroom.
Van Helsing finds that Lucy is still alive, and he orders brandy and warmth to revive her.
Seward wakes the maids, who prepare hot water and fire, and Lucy is placed in a warm bath to recover.
Quincey Morris appears on the sofa, having been sent by Arthur's telegram, and offers to give his blood.
Quincey gives blood in a third transfusion, and Lucy's heart and lungs improve under morphia.
Van Helsing shows Seward a paper that fell from Lucy's breast, and Seward is bewildered by its contents.
Seward plans to certify Mrs. Westenra's death as heart disease to avoid an inquest.
Seward arranges for the undertaker to measure for the coffin and registers the death.
Quincey asks Seward what is wrong with Lucy, and Seward admits that Arthur gave blood first and that Lucy has had several transfusions.
Lucy wakes, grieves her mother, and in her sleep tears up the paper Van Helsing had replaced in her breast.
Arthur arrives at Hillingham and Lucy briefly rallies to speak with him.
Van Helsing and Arthur rest while Seward takes the night watch, and Lucy's teeth appear sharper as she sleeps.
At dawn Van Helsing discovers that the wounds on Lucy's throat have disappeared and declares that she is dying.
Lucy wakes in a changed, voluptuous state and asks Arthur to kiss her, but Van Helsing pulls him away.
Lucy asks Van Helsing to guard Arthur and give her peace, and Van Helsing swears an oath to protect him.
Lucy dies, and Seward leads the grieving Arthur away.
Van Helsing tells Seward that Lucy's death is only the beginning and that they must wait and see.
Mr. Marquand reports that Mrs. Westenra left her whole estate to Arthur, which the family's lawyers had tried to prevent.
Arthur visits the death-chamber, grief-stricken, and kisses Lucy's dead hand and forehead before saying goodbye.
Seward reassures Arthur that Lucy's face has softened in death, and Arthur takes his leave of her.
Van Helsing tells the undertaker's men to proceed with the coffin preparations.
Van Helsing reveals that the gold crucifix placed on Lucy's mouth was stolen in the night and recovered from the thief, so the operation is called off.
Van Helsing asks Arthur to trust him fully and to allow him to keep Lucy's papers and letters, and Arthur agrees.
Van Helsing keeps watch through the night near Lucy's coffin, which is strewn with wild garlic flowers.
Mina and Jonathan attend the funeral of Mr. Hawkins and feel the loss of their friend.
Jonathan sees the dark, cruel stranger in Piccadilly and, terrified, says it is the man himself.
Jonathan falls asleep on Mina's shoulder in Green Park and wakes without remembering the stranger.
Mina receives a telegram from Van Helsing announcing the deaths of Mrs. Westenra and Lucy, both buried that day.
Arthur returns to Ring with Quincey Morris after the burial.
Van Helsing confides in Seward that he laughs out of grief and says he knows a reason for his sorrow he cannot share.
The group scatters, and Lucy is laid to rest in the family tomb.
Mina sends a telegram inviting Van Helsing to come to Exeter and see her.
Mina expects Van Helsing's visit concerns Lucy's sleepwalking and her last illness rather than Jonathan.
Mina gives Van Helsing her shorthand diary, then hands him a typewritten copy of it instead.
Van Helsing says Mina's diary has opened a gate for him and that he will serve her and those she loves.
Mina, overwhelmed, implores Van Helsing to make Jonathan well again, and he comforts her.
Mina gives Van Helsing a typewritten copy of Jonathan's journal abroad to read and judge.
Van Helsing writes that Jonathan's journal is true and that Jonathan's brain and heart are sound.
Mina learns Jonathan will return that night and asks Van Helsing to come to breakfast the next morning.
Jonathan resumes his journal, reassured by Van Helsing's verdict and no longer afraid even of the Count.
Jonathan tells Van Helsing that his doubts were lifted by Van Helsing's letter and that he now trusts his senses.
Van Helsing asks Jonathan to tell him what happened before his trip to Transylvania, and Jonathan agrees to help.
Van Helsing sees something in the Westminster Gazette, turns pale, and leaves on the train, murmuring that it has come so soon.
Van Helsing returns from Exeter and hands Seward the Westminster Gazette, pointing to a report of children with throat wounds.
Van Helsing describes vampire-like bats and long-lived creatures, and suggests the children's wounds were made by Lucy.
Van Helsing declares that the wounds in the children's throats were made by Lucy, shocking Seward.
Van Helsing reveals to Seward that Lucy is Un-Dead, and asks him to accompany him to prove it.
Van Helsing and Seward visit the injured child at the hospital, and Dr. Vincent shows them punctures like Lucy's.
Van Helsing and Seward enter the Westenra tomb at night and open Lucy's coffin, finding it empty.
In the churchyard Van Helsing takes a sleeping child from a white figure, and they leave the child on the Heath for a policeman to find.
Van Helsing reopens the tomb and shows Seward that Lucy's body lies there, fresh and unchanged, with sharpened teeth.
Van Helsing decides to delay the staking, leaves a note in case he does not return, and plans to meet the men at the hotel.
Seward resumes doubt in the morning and resolves to watch Van Helsing carefully.
Arthur and Quincey meet Van Helsing, who asks their promise to act on his plan without knowing its details.
Van Helsing tells Arthur that Lucy may be Un-Dead, and Arthur reluctantly agrees to go with him to wait.
Drove the stake through Lucy's heart in the tomb and was left exhausted; has now kissed her and forgiven Van Helsing.
The men open Lucy's coffin and find it empty, shaking their trust in Van Helsing's account.
Lucy appears in the churchyard with a child in her arms, her face hardened and her mouth bloody.
Lucy drops the child and tries to lure Arthur to her, but Van Helsing holds up his crucifix and she is driven back from the tomb.
Van Helsing seals the tomb with the Host and Lucy's body re-enters through a gap too small for a knife.
The men return to the churchyard at night, dressed in black, and wait until the gates are locked.
Van Helsing explains the curse of the Un-Dead and asks who should drive the stake, and Arthur volunteers.
Arthur drives the stake into Lucy's heart while Van Helsing reads the prayers for the dead, and the body writhes and then lies still.
Lucy's body appears peaceful and as she was in life, and Arthur kisses her after the staking.
The men cut off Lucy's head, fill her mouth with garlic, solder the leaden coffin shut, and Arthur keeps the tomb key.
Van Helsing asks the men to help him find the author of their sorrow, and each swears to continue to the end.
Van Helsing arranges to meet Seward and Arthur for dinner in two nights, promising to reveal his plans, and leaves for Amsterdam.
Seward meets Mina at Paddington and brings her to his asylum.
Seward refuses to tell Mina of Lucy's death, then gives her the phonograph cylinders to hear.
Mina persuades Seward to let her share the whole record, and he agrees.
Mina listens to the account of Lucy's death and is overcome, then begins typing it.
Seward sees Renfield, who seems unusually sane and speaks of going home, which makes Seward suspicious.
Jonathan goes to Whitby and learns the boxes were delivered to Carfax.
Jonathan traces the consignment through King's Cross and Carter, Paterson & Co., whose men describe the dusty Carfax house.
Lord Godalming and Quincey Morris arrive early and Mina tells them she has read and typed the whole record.
Lord Godalming breaks down in grief and Mina comforts him, and he promises lasting brotherly friendship.
Mina offers Morris comfort, and he kisses her hand and calls her little girl.
Godalming and Morris arrive at Seward's house and study the transcribed diaries and letters that Harker and Mina arranged.
Mina visits Renfield at Seward's invitation, and Renfield's manner shifts from odd to philosophical while he speaks with her.
Renfield tells Mina he hopes never to see her again and blesses her.
Van Helsing arrives and learns from Seward that Dracula's house is next to Seward's own.
Van Helsing reads Mina's record and encourages her to let it stand, and the full record is completed.
The council convenes, with Van Helsing at the head of the table and Mina as secretary.
Van Helsing lays out the vampire's powers and history, and the dangers of failure.
Morris, Godalming, Harker and Seward pledge themselves to the campaign, joining hands around Van Helsing's crucifix.
Van Helsing details the vampire's weaknesses and the means of destroying him.
Morris leaves the room, and a shot is fired outside the window, shattering the glass.
The council decides to trace the fifty boxes of earth and find the vampire's lair.
The men decide to keep Mina out of the danger and to go to the house at Carfax without her.
Renfield asks urgently to see Seward, prompting the men to follow him to his room.
Renfield asks to be released, arguing his sanity and invoking a higher duty.
Seward refuses Renfield's request for release, which leads to an outburst from the patient.
Renfield asks Seward to recall that he tried to convince him that night.
The men enter the chapel of the Carfax house, where the stench is overwhelming, and find twenty-nine of the fifty earth-boxes still there.
Rats swarm the chapel, and Lord Godalming releases the terriers, which drive the rats off.
The men search the rest of the house and find nothing but dust, and the dogs show no unease.
Van Helsing concludes that twenty-one boxes are now known to be removed and that the Count is elsewhere.
Van Helsing visits Renfield, who insults him and refuses to talk, ending any chance of learning from him.
Mina weeps and reflects that her visit to Whitby led to Lucy's death, and resolves to hide her distress from Jonathan.
Mina has a frightening dream of a pillar of mist entering the room and a pale face bending over her.
Mina takes a sleeping draught from Seward, fearing she may lose the power to wake.
Harker learns from Smollet the destinations of the twelve boxes delivered from Carfax, to Chicksand Street and Jamaica Lane.
Harker decides to keep the investigation hidden from Mina, to protect her health.
Harker traces Sam Bloxam to a cold-storage building at Poplar and learns of nine boxes taken to a Piccadilly house.
Bloxam reveals the old man helping him carry the boxes lifted them with unnatural ease, suggesting the Count handles the earth himself.
Harker finds the Piccadilly house empty and decides it is the next lair of the Count.
Mitchell, Sons & Candy refuse to name the buyer but agree to write to Lord Godalming, who Harker claims is the inquirer.
The men decide to wait for the agents' letter before taking any action.
Seward finds Renfield in a superior, cunning mood, speaking of life and souls as if he expects something.
Renfield says he will never lack the means of life, suggesting an assurance from an outside source.
Renfield ignores Van Helsing and Seward, singing and folding a notebook, revealing nothing.
Mitchell, Sons & Candy write that a Count de Ville bought No. 347 Piccadilly for cash.
Seward posts a man in the corridor to monitor Renfield's room overnight.
Renfield is found bloodied on the floor after a wild yell in his room.
Renfield is found on the floor of his room, badly injured, his face beaten and his back apparently broken.
Seward calls Van Helsing, who arrives and decides an operation is needed, sending the attendant away.
Arthur and Quincey arrive at the door, having been woken by the attendant's call, and join the vigil.
Van Helsing trephines Renfield's skull, and Renfield wakes briefly, lucid and in agony.
Renfield confesses that the Count came to his window, promised him life, and that he was called in and let him enter.
Renfield says he resisted the Count, who flung him down and fled under the door, and that the Count drained Mina.
The company arms themselves with the same tools as before and rushes to the Harkers' room.
They break in and find the Count feeding on Mina while Jonathan lies in a stupor; the Count flees as Van Helsing raises the Sacred Wafer.
Jonathan wakes to find his wife's blood on herself, and Mina is shamed and sobs, saying she is now unclean.
Seward tells Jonathan what happened, and Arthur reports that the Count burned the manuscript and the phonograph cylinders and that Renfield is dead.
Morris reports seeing a bat fly westward from Renfield's window, suggesting the Count has gone to another lair.
Mina describes how the Count drank from her, forced her to drink his blood, and vowed that she must come to his call.
Renfield is found dead on the floor with broken neck bones, and the attendant reports hearing voices and Renfield crying out to God.
The company agrees that Mina will be told everything, and she accepts this despite her grief.
Van Helsing forbids Mina to die by any hand, including her own, until the Count is destroyed, and she promises to try to live.
Van Helsing plans to hunt down the Count's remaining lairs during the daylight hours, when he cannot change form.
Mina insists that the men go to Piccadilly, and the group prepares to split its forces.
As Van Helsing places the Sacred Wafer on Mina's forehead, it burns her flesh, leaving a scar.
The men pledge to lift the sorrow from Mina, and all kneel and swear to be true to each other.
The group enters Carfax and sterilises the earth boxes there by placing Sacred Wafers in them.
The group finds the Count's papers and keys, and Godalming and Morris leave with the keys to destroy the other boxes.
A telegram from Mina warns that the Count has left Carfax heading south and may come to see them.
Godalming and Morris return, reporting they destroyed the boxes at both places.
The Count bursts into the room, Harker strikes at him, and the Count escapes through the window and into the stable.
The Count vows revenge over centuries and fastens the stable door behind him.
Van Helsing pockets the remaining gold, takes the title-deeds and burns the rest of the papers.
The men search the yard and mews but find no sign of the Count.
Van Helsing says one earth-box remains unfound and that they must return to protect Mina.
Mina comforts Harker, who is in despair at the hunt's failure.
Mina begs the men to show pity toward the Count even as they destroy him.
Harker vows to destroy the Count's life, and Mina pleads with him not to speak so.
Quincey, Godalming and Seward divide the night watch over Mina.
Mina wakes Harker, and he finds Morris on guard in the corridor.
Mina asks for Van Helsing to hypnotise her before dawn so she can speak.
Van Helsing hypnotises Mina, who describes being on a ship with the sound of water and men at work.
Van Helsing concludes the Count has fled London by ship and resolves to pursue him.
Van Helsing warns Mina that the Count's mark on her throat makes her time now dangerous.
Mina faints as Van Helsing speaks.
Van Helsing tells Harker by phonograph that the Count has fled to Transylvania and that the company will pursue him.
Van Helsing's party traces the Count to the Czarina Catherine, a ship sailing for Varna, and learns of the box he shipped.
A fog delays the ship's departure, and the Count returns briefly to see where his box was stowed before the vessel sails on the ebb tide.
Mina insists on joining the journey, saying the Count may compel her to reveal the plans, and Van Helsing agrees.
Van Helsing argues the Count must be destroyed to save Mina and humanity, and the company resolves to leave for Varna by the 17th.
Van Helsing compares the Count to a man-eating tiger that will not give up its hunt.
The company agrees to travel to Varna with Winchesters and plans to board the ship there and destroy the box.
Van Helsing assumes Harker will stay behind with Mina, a plan Harker does not yet accept.
Harker is left unsure of his wife's refusal to join the discussions, which makes him uneasy.
Mina makes Harker promise on his word of honour not to tell her of the plans against the Count.
Mina asks Van Helsing to come, and tells him she must go on the journey since she will be drawn to the Count's will.
Morris vows to destroy the Count's box at once, no matter who is watching.
Harker makes his will, naming Mina his sole heir and the others as the remainder.
Mina enters her wakeful state at sunrise and sunset, and the company learns to expect these moments of freedom.
Mina asks that if she is becoming the Count's creature, the company should end her life, and they all swear to do so.
Quincey Morris swears to Mina that he will kill her if the time comes and to make certain of it.
The company reaches Varna and books rooms at the Odessus hotel, while Lord Godalming checks at the Consulate for telegrams.
The company plans to board the ship between sunrise and sunset, when the Count cannot leave his box, and destroy him.
Godalming obtains permission from the shippers and the agent to open the box, and the company agrees on a plan to behead and stake the Count.
Lloyd's reports that the Czarina Catherine was sighted at the Dardanelles, which brings the ship close to Varna.
Mina's trance reports show the Count hurrying toward his destination.
A telegram reports the Czarina Catherine entering Galatz at one o'clock, so the ship has passed Varna and the company learns the box has not reached them.
Mina reveals she knows the train times and that the only train to Galatz leaves at 6:30 the next morning.
Van Helsing assigns each man a task for the journey to Galatz and keeps Mina with him to report her trances.
Van Helsing reveals to Seward that the Count may have reached into Mina's mind during the trance and that he means to use this knowledge.
Mina realises the Count's selfish, limited mind has cut himself off from her, and she feels her soul freer than since the night he marked her.
Van Helsing argues that the Count's selfishness will be his undoing, and asks that the company's account be written down for the men's return.
Travels with Van Helsing toward the Borgo Pass, carrying a revolver and wearing fur coats for the cold.
Accepts Mina's deduction about the route and plans to take her into the Count's country by the Borgo Pass.
Travels by steam launch with Lord Godalming up the river in pursuit of the box.
Believed to have arranged the river carriage of the box through Skinsky and then silenced him.
Mina's hypnotic trance describes a ship at rest with men calling and a light appearing, suggesting the vessel is near land.
Van Helsing explains the Count must reach land before dawn or be exposed, so the company must find him on the water.
Mina's morning trance reports only darkness, lapping water and creaking wood before sunrise, and the company must wait for night.
Mina reports cattle lowing and a strange sound, then breaks off and turns pale in her trance.
Mina wakes unaware of what she has said and is surprised at Van Helsing's stern order to speak.
At Galatz, Van Helsing, Seward and Harker visit the agents and board the Czarina Catherine, meeting its skipper.
The skipper reveals a box was delivered before dawn to Immanuel Hildesheim under the name of Count Dracula.
Hildesheim passes the box to Petrof Skinsky, whom the company then fails to find, losing the trail.
Skinsky's body is found in St. Peter churchyard with the throat torn open, likely a wild animal's work, and the company is left stranded.
Seward releases Harker from his promise to keep Mina out of the affair, as the danger grows.
Mina deduces the Count's box is travelling by river in an open boat, probably up the Pruth or Sereth.
Mina identifies the Bistritza loop as the water route nearest the Count's castle.
Van Helsing and the men resolve to hunt the box by river and road, with Godalming and Harker by launch and Seward and Morris on horseback.
Van Helsing resolves to take Mina overland toward the Count's castle while the men pursue the box on the water.
Mina and Van Helsing leave by train for Veresti, planning to drive to the Borgo Pass.
Godalming and Harker set off upstream in the launch, expecting the box to go up the Sereth and Bistritza.
The launch passes open boats on the river; none carries a box of the size they seek.
At Fundu they fly a Roumanian flag, which earns deference from other boats, but they hear of a fast big boat passing in the night.
Seward and Morris ride three days on the road with horses, pressing on toward the launch.
The launch is delayed by an accident on the rapids, repaired by Godalming, and resumes the chase.
Van Helsing buys a carriage and horses at Veresti while Mina waits, with about seventy miles to cover.
Dies at sunset, crumbling to dust after Jonathan Harker and Quincey Morris strike his throat and heart.
Van Helsing and Mina drive all day toward the Borgo Pass, changing horses and recording the boat's position through hypnosis.
Van Helsing reaches the Borgo Pass with Mina, who directs the way and seems to know the road from Jonathan's diary.
At night the vampire women materialise in the snow and call Mina to join them, but she stays within the Holy circle.
Van Helsing climbs to the castle, searches the chapel, and finds three vampire women sleeping in their tombs.
Van Helsing destroys the three women by staking and beheading them, then banishes Dracula from his tomb with the Sacred Wafer.
Van Helsing returns to Mina, who urges him to leave the castle and go east to meet Jonathan.
Mina and Van Helsing set out eastward on foot, finding a rocky hollow to shelter in as wolves howl nearby.
From the rock they see the gypsy cart with the box and spot Jonathan, Godalming, Seward and Morris racing to intercept it.
The four men halt the gypsies with rifles, and the gypsy leader orders his men to fight.
Jonathan flings the great box to the ground, and Morris and Jonathan pry off the lid as the sun nears the mountains.
Jonathan's knife cuts the Count's throat and Morris's bowie knife pierces his heart at sunset, and the body crumbles to dust.
Morris, mortally wounded in the side, takes Mina's hand and speaks of the curse passing away before he dies.
The companions gather the papers from their safe and realise there is almost no authentic document among them, only typed records and private note-books.
Van Helsing declares that no proof is needed and that the boy will one day understand what his mother and her devoted friends endured for her sake.
